query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a reactive dopant (e.g., ~1–2 at% Ti) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a robust, self-healing nanocrystalline oxide layer during sliding that acts as an adaptive lubricating glaze, thereby maintaining both a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a standard, coarse-grained microstructure that shows increased friction and wear at higher sliding temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace reactive element (Ti) into the alloy composition (~1–2 at%), which is expected to oxidize during sliding and trigger formation of a continuous, protective and adaptive oxide nanocomposite layer.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests under variable load and sliding speeds, evaluated over a wide temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline oxide layer (or glaze) formed in situ on the alloy surface that is self-renewing during wear.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, frictional heating activates the oxidation of the Ti dopant. The resulting oxide forms a dense nanocomposite surface layer that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, accommodates plastic deformation, and adapts its structure to changing temperatures, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped CoCrFeNi, the Ti-doped alloy will show a statistically lower and more stable friction coefficient and a reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range, particularly at elevated temperatures where oxidation mechanisms dominate.
generation.baseline: Undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which exhibits increased friction and wear (due to plastic deformation and unstable oxide formation) as temperature rises toward 800 °C.
generation.boundary: Tested under dry sliding conditions with typical loads and speeds that generate sufficient frictional heat to induce oxidation, within the environmental limits of RT to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and the precise nature of the oxide layer (its phase composition and stability) require further optimization; the effect under different sliding conditions and loads may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of standard CoCrFeNi alloy and one set alloyed with ~1–2 at% Ti. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding tests at room temperature, intermediate temperatures, and up to 800 °C under the same applied loads and sliding speeds. Monitor the surface evolution during sliding.
measurements: Wear rate determination via 3D profilometry of wear tracks
Post-test microstructural analysis using SEM/EDS and XRD to characterize the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped samples do not exhibit a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to the undoped specimens across the temperature range, or if no continuous nanocrystalline oxide layer is observable, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals. The high wear resistance of the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy is achieved by the synergistic effect of the low friction coefficient (~0.09) of the alloy and the in-situ formation of an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface, which exhibits a high strength and homogeneous plastic flow behavior.
